sections.title: Taxonomy and model organism
sections.text: Neurospora crassa Shear & B.O. Dodge is a filamentous mold in the phylum Ascomycota, class Sordariomycetes, order Sordariales and family Sordariaceae. It is a haploid model organism long used in genetics and cell biology. Its orange mold-like appearance in culture comes from a microscopic growth and sporulation phase; it is not a mushroom with a cap.

sections.title: Hyphae and asexual spores
sections.text: The mycelium is a network of branching tubular hyphae divided by porous septa that allow cytoplasm to pass between compartments. Under the Fungal Genetics Stock Center’s (FGSC) reference conditions, hyphae are about 8–15 µm in diameter. Aerial hyphae form conidiophores that produce dispersal conidia. Macroconidia, often the most abundant, are spherical and about 5–8 µm in diameter; they usually contain two or three nuclei, although counts vary. Smaller uninucleate microconidia (about 2.5–3.5 µm) are also produced. Masses of conidia give cultures their characteristic orange color.

sections.title: Perithecia, asci and ascospores
sections.text: Sexual reproduction in N. crassa requires contact between compatible mating types. It produces flask-shaped microscopic fruiting bodies called perithecia, each with a neck and an apical opening (ostiole), about 400–500 µm in diameter. Each contains many elongated asci, typically 180–200 × 15–18 µm; a mature ascus holds eight linearly arranged ascospores. Mature ascospores are dark, thick-walled and marked by longitudinal ridges; the FGSC lists them at about 27–30 × 13–15 µm. They are discharged through the ostiole.

sections.title: Ecology and illustration scale
sections.text: In nature, sporulating Neurospora is often observed on burned or charred plant material after fires, including sugarcane residues. A 2025 study found that N. crassa degraded uncharred grass residues better than strongly heat-treated material; post-fire growth therefore does not show that the fungus feeds on char itself. Its natural lifestyle remains under investigation. The accompanying image is an explanatory microscopic schematic, not to scale: hyphae and conidia, an opened perithecium and a detailed ascus are shown side by side so structures of very different sizes remain legible.

traits: Orange filamentous mold; its mycelium is microscopic, and aerial conidia give colonies their visible color
Branching hyphae about 8–15 µm in diameter; conidiophores bear macroconidia about 5–8 µm across and smaller microconidia
Spherical macroconidia, usually with two or three nuclei; smaller microconidia are uninucleate
Sexual perithecia are flask-shaped and about 0.4–0.5 mm in diameter, with a neck and apical ostiole
Elongated asci each contain eight linearly ordered ascospores; mature spores are dark, longitudinally ridged and discharged through the ostiole
Often observed on burned plant material after fires; its natural ecological strategy remains under study
safetyNote: This entry describes a microscopic species and model organism; it cannot identify an unknown mold or assess the food safety of contaminated food.
